explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. Ezekiel, a priest living among the exiles, says it himself: "the heavens opened and I saw visions of God." (Ezekiel 1:1) He doesn't say he heard about it from somebody else. He saw it with his own eyes, right there by the river.
It's actually true, friend. Ezekiel says, "the heavens opened and I saw visions of God." (Ezekiel 1:1) So the opening heavens aren't just some weather event. What he sees there is God's own visions.

Fire it is, friend. Ezekiel sees "a great cloud with fire flashing back and forth and brilliant light all around it." (Ezekiel 1:4) Back and forth, over and over, like it can't sit still. I've seen my oven act up, but never like that.

Hail is a fair guess for a stormy cloud, friend. But the text says nothing about hail. It says the cloud has fire flashing back and forth, with brilliant light all around it. I'd stay off the ice and watch the fire.
Snow would make this a very different vision, friend. Ezekiel doesn't see a cold cloud at all. He sees "a great cloud with fire flashing back and forth." (Ezekiel 1:4) That's fire, not flurries.

Hands, friend. "Under their wings on their four sides they had human hands." (Ezekiel 1:8) That fits with the human form Ezekiel noticed when he first described them. Tucked under the wings on all four sides, that's a lot of hands.

Claws would match some of the other things Ezekiel sees, friend, but not this. The text says the creatures have a human form, and under their wings are human hands. Claws never come up in the passage. It's hands, all the way around.

Tails are not in this vision, friend. Ezekiel lists faces, wings, straight legs and feet like a calf's hooves. Then he says that under their wings on four sides they had human hands. No tails anywhere in the description.
Not quite, friend. The text says the opposite: "They did not turn as they moved; each one went straight ahead." (Ezekiel 1:9) No turning at all. Whichever way they're headed, they just go.

Yes, friend, it's false. Ezekiel says, "They did not turn as they moved; each one went straight ahead." (Ezekiel 1:9) He says it again in verse 12. Everything about the way they move is straight ahead.

That's the set, friend. Each one has a man's face, and also "the face of a lion on the right side, the face of an ox on the left side, and also the face of an eagle." (Ezekiel 1:10) Four faces on one creature. And I sometimes can't keep up with my one face on a Monday.

Those are animals, friend, but not the ones Ezekiel sees. The text names a lion on the right side, an ox on the left side, and an eagle. (Ezekiel 1:10) The man's face comes first. No bear, goat or dove in this one.

Close in spirit, friend, but the text names different animals. Ezekiel says the creature has the face of a lion on the right side, an ox on the left side, and an eagle. (Ezekiel 1:10) A man's face comes with them. That's the full list.
You got it, friend. "Wherever the spirit would go, they would go, without turning as they moved." (Ezekiel 1:12) The creatures don't wander off on their own. They go where the spirit goes.

The cloud is where Ezekiel's vision starts, friend, so I see why you picked it. But the text says what decides their direction: "Wherever the spirit would go, they would go." (Ezekiel 1:12) The cloud isn't named for that.

Ezekiel is the one watching, friend. He's looking and describing, and the text never has him steering anything. What it says is, "Wherever the spirit would go, they would go, without turning as they moved." (Ezekiel 1:12) The spirit sets the direction.

explanations.answer: As quick as flashes of lightning
explanations.explanation: Fast as lightning, friend. "The creatures were darting back and forth as quickly as flashes of lightning." (Ezekiel 1:14) Blink and you miss it. I can't even find my oven mitts that quickly.

explanations.answer: As quick as a running deer
explanations.explanation: A deer is fast, friend, but Ezekiel reaches higher. He says the creatures were darting back and forth "as quickly as flashes of lightning." (Ezekiel 1:14) That's the comparison the text gives.

explanations.answer: As quick as a falling star
explanations.explanation: A falling star is a fun picture, friend, but it's not the one in the text. Ezekiel says they were darting back and forth "as quickly as flashes of lightning." (Ezekiel 1:14) Lightning is the comparison.
A wheel, friend. Ezekiel says, "I saw a wheel on the ground beside each creature with its four faces." (Ezekiel 1:15) One wheel for each creature. And he's only getting started describing them.
A lampstand is a good guess with all that fire around, friend. But Ezekiel doesn't see one. He sees a wheel on the ground beside each creature. (Ezekiel 1:15)
Ezekiel is a priest, so an altar would make sense in his world, friend. But the text puts something else on the ground beside each creature: a wheel. (Ezekiel 1:15) No altar in this vision.

True, friend. "As they moved, they went in any of the four directions, without pivoting as they moved." (Ezekiel 1:17) No turning around first, they just go. I can't even back out of a parking spot that smoothly.
It's true, friend. The text says, "As they moved, they went in any of the four directions, without pivoting as they moved." (Ezekiel 1:17) So the wheels go any of the four ways with no pivoting.
Not so, friend. Ezekiel says, "when the creatures rose from the ground, the wheels also rose." (Ezekiel 1:19) The wheels don't stay behind. They go up right alongside the creatures.
Right, it's false. "When the creatures rose from the ground, the wheels also rose." (Ezekiel 1:19) Ezekiel says it again in verse 21. The wheels never stay behind.

explanations.answer: The spirit of the creatures is in the wheels
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says, friend. The wheels rise alongside them "because the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels." (Ezekiel 1:20) So they move together because of that. Ezekiel gives that reason twice, in verses 20 and 21.

explanations.answer: The wheels are fastened to the creatures' feet
explanations.explanation: That's a neat guess, friend, but the text never says anything is fastened. The wheels are "beside" the creatures. What it gives as the reason is that "the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels." (Ezekiel 1:20)

explanations.answer: The creatures lift the wheels with their hands
explanations.explanation: Hands are under the creatures' wings, friend, but the text never has them lifting anything. The reason Ezekiel gives is that "the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels." (Ezekiel 1:20) That's why they rise together.

That's right, friend. "When they stood still, they lowered their wings." (Ezekiel 1:24) Moving, the wings sound like roaring waters. Standing still, they come down. Then a voice comes from above the expanse. (Ezekiel 1:25)

It's true, friend. The text says, "When they stood still, they lowered their wings." (Ezekiel 1:24) Then in verse 25 a voice comes from above the expanse while they stand there with their wings lowered.

A throne, friend. "Above the expanse over their heads was the likeness of a throne with the appearance of sapphire." (Ezekiel 1:26) Notice Ezekiel says likeness and appearance. He's careful with his words, and I think that's because it's a lot to take in.
A mountain feels big enough for this scene, friend. But Ezekiel sees something else above the expanse: the likeness of a throne with the appearance of sapphire. (Ezekiel 1:26)
A pillar is a sturdy guess, friend. The text doesn't put one up there, though. Above the expanse is "the likeness of a throne with the appearance of sapphire." (Ezekiel 1:26)

explanations.answer: A figure like that of a man
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. "On the throne high above was a figure like that of a man." (Ezekiel 1:26) Ezekiel says "like" a man. He's describing what he sees as carefully as he can.

explanations.answer: A figure like that of a lamb
explanations.explanation: A lamb is a good guess, friend, but it isn't what the text says here. On the throne, Ezekiel sees "a figure like that of a man." (Ezekiel 1:26) That's the description.

explanations.answer: A figure like that of a dove
explanations.explanation: A dove doesn't show up on this throne, friend. The text says that on the throne high above was "a figure like that of a man." (Ezekiel 1:26)

A rainbow, friend. "The appearance of the brilliant light all around Him was like that of a rainbow in a cloud on a rainy day." (Ezekiel 1:28) Rainbows are my favorite color, so you know I'm glad it made the list.

A sunbeam is a nice picture, friend. But the text puts it in a rainy-day cloud, and there it's like a rainbow. (Ezekiel 1:28) Rain and sunbeams can go together, but that isn't the comparison Ezekiel makes.
I'm partial to stars, friend. Every finished cookie box lights one in my sky. But Ezekiel says the brilliant light around Him was like a rainbow in a cloud on a rainy day. (Ezekiel 1:28)
That's what he does, friend. "When I saw it, I fell facedown and heard a voice speaking." (Ezekiel 1:28) I think it was a lot to take in. And notice he's listening even from the ground.
It's a loud vision, friend, but Ezekiel doesn't shout. The text says, "I fell facedown and heard a voice speaking." (Ezekiel 1:28) He goes down, and then he hears.
I'd have been tempted, friend. But Ezekiel doesn't run. The text says, "I fell facedown and heard a voice speaking." (Ezekiel 1:28) He stays right where he is.
